playlist.title: How LLMs Work: Foundations
playlist.description:
Short videos on the math and code behind large language models: vectors, dot products, matrices, nonlinearity, exponentials and logs, probability, softmax, statistics, waves, gradients, NumPy, neural networks, autograd and train/validation data. Each video points to the How LLMs Work episodes that use it.

Study guides (PDF) and source code: https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos

episodes.title: Vectors: Lists of Numbers as Arrows | How LLMs Work: Foundations F01
episodes.description:
The basic building block of every LLM.

Study guide for this lesson (PDF): https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos/blob/main/foundations/study/f01_study.pdf
All lessons, study guides and source code: https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos

This video has one big idea: a vector is a list of numbers that you can also picture as an arrow. You can add vectors, stretch them and measure their length, and the rules are the same whether a vector has 2 numbers or 768. Every token inside an LLM is represented by one.

Chapters
0:00 A vector is a list of numbers
0:27 Two numbers, one arrow
0:51 Adding vectors
1:02 Scaling: stretch, shrink, flip
1:13 Length, by Pythagoras · Directions that mean something
1:32 Vectors in NumPy

Foundations F01, a pre-series for How LLMs Work. Used in episodes 1, 3, 4 and 9.

episodes.title: The Dot Product | How LLMs Work: Foundations F02
episodes.description:
One number that says how much two vectors agree.

Study guide for this lesson (PDF): https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos/blob/main/foundations/study/f02_study.pdf
All lessons, study guides and source code: https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos

This video has one big idea: the dot product turns two vectors into one number that says how much they point the same way. The recipe is multiply matching numbers, then add. Divide by both lengths and you get cosine similarity, a pure measure of direction. LLMs use dot products almost everywhere.

Chapters
0:00 Multiply matching numbers, then add
0:37 Positive, zero, negative: agreement
0:50 The shadow and the angle
1:07 Cosine similarity
1:21 Dot products everywhere
1:33 The dot product in NumPy

episodes.title: Matrices: Many Dot Products at Once | How LLMs Work: Foundations F03
episodes.description:
The table of numbers behind every layer.

Study guide for this lesson (PDF): https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos/blob/main/foundations/study/f03_study.pdf
All lessons, study guides and source code: https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos

This video has one big idea: a matrix is a table of numbers that does many dot products at once. Matrix times vector dots every row with the vector; matrix times matrix dots every row with every column. That is how one layer of an LLM transforms every token in a single step.

0:25 Matrix times vector
0:36 A matrix transforms space
0:47 The shapes must line up
0:58 Matrix times matrix: every token at once

episodes.title: Straight Lines and Bends | How LLMs Work: Foundations F04
episodes.description:
Linear functions, and why networks need a bend.

Study guide for this lesson (PDF): https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos/blob/main/foundations/study/f04_study.pdf
All lessons, study guides and source code: https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos

This video has one big idea: linear layers alone are not enough. A matrix can stretch and rotate, but a stack of matrices is always just one more matrix. Putting a simple bend between the layers, a nonlinear function like ReLU or GELU, is what lets a neural network build curved, complicated functions.

Chapters
0:00 Linear: double in, double out
0:28 Linear layers collapse into one
0:38 What a straight map can't do
0:51 The fix: a bend called ReLU
1:08 GELU: a smooth ReLU
1:20 Curves from many straight pieces · A layer in code

episodes.title: Exponentials and Logarithms | How LLMs Work: Foundations F05
episodes.description:
Fast growth, and the function that undoes it.

Study guide for this lesson (PDF): https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos/blob/main/foundations/study/f05_study.pdf
All lessons, study guides and source code: https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos

This video is about two functions that appear all over LLMs. The exponential eˣ grows by multiplying: it is always positive, and it turns small differences into big ones. The logarithm ln x undoes it: it turns probabilities into negative numbers that are easy to compare, and it turns multiplication into addition.

Chapters
0:00 Growth by multiplying
0:26 The number e, and eˣ is always positive
0:47 eˣ exaggerates differences
1:00 The logarithm undoes the exponential
1:13 Logs of probabilities
1:29 Multiplication becomes addition
1:41 exp and log in NumPy

episodes.title: Probability and Sampling | How LLMs Work: Foundations F06
episodes.description:
Distributions, weighted dice, and randomness.

Study guide for this lesson (PDF): https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos/blob/main/foundations/study/f06_study.pdf
All lessons, study guides and source code: https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos

This video is about what an LLM actually outputs: not a word, but a probability distribution over words. You will see what a probability is, why a distribution adds up to one, how sampling picks one word at random according to it (a weighted spinner), and how a seed makes that randomness repeatable.

Chapters

0:26 A distribution adds up to one
0:43 Sampling: a weighted spinner
0:53 Many spins match the probabilities · Why sample? Variety
1:10 Seeds make randomness repeatable

episodes.title: Softmax, Properly | How LLMs Work: Foundations F07
episodes.description:
From any scores to probabilities.

Study guide for this lesson (PDF): https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos/blob/main/foundations/study/f07_study.pdf
All lessons, study guides and source code: https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos

This video has one big idea: softmax turns any list of scores into probabilities, in two steps. Exponentiate every score, then divide by the total. Everything else follows from those two steps: why it is “soft”, why only the differences between scores matter, how temperature sharpens or flattens the result, and why code subtracts the largest score first.

Chapters
0:00 Scores in, probabilities out
0:36 Working it through: 3, 2, 0
0:51 A soft version of the max
1:02 Only the differences matter · Temperature: sharper or flatter
1:20 Subtract the max: softmax in code

episodes.title: Averages and Spread | How LLMs Work: Foundations F08
episodes.description:
Mean, standard deviation, and keeping numbers tame.

Study guide for this lesson (PDF): https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos/blob/main/foundations/study/f08_study.pdf
All lessons, study guides and source code: https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos

This video has one big idea: two simple statistics describe a list of numbers, the mean (its center) and the standard deviation (its spread), and together they let us keep numbers tame. Normalizing with them is what layer norm does, and the same idea of spread explains why attention divides its scores by √d.

Chapters
0:00 The mean: the center
0:28 Standard deviation: the typical distance
0:52 Normalizing: mean 0, spread 1
1:14 The spread of a sum grows like √n
1:26 Dividing by √d keeps softmax tame

episodes.title: Waves and Rotations | How LLMs Work: Foundations F09
episodes.description:
Sine, cosine, and turning arrows.

Study guide for this lesson (PDF): https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos/blob/main/foundations/study/f09_study.pdf
All lessons, study guides and source code: https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos

This video has one big idea: sine and cosine come from a point moving around a circle. Its height traces a wave that repeats every full turn, 2π, and the same two functions can turn an arrow by any angle without changing its length. Episode 4 uses both: waves of different frequencies to mark positions, and rotations that turn relative position into a relative angle.

Chapters

0:25 The sine wave, and a full turn of 2π
0:47 Frequency: how fast it repeats
0:58 Many waves: a fingerprint for every position · Rotating an arrow

episodes.title: Slopes and Gradients | How LLMs Work: Foundations F10
episodes.description:
How a model knows which way to adjust.

Study guide for this lesson (PDF): https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos/blob/main/foundations/study/f10_study.pdf
All lessons, study guides and source code: https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos

This video answers one question: when a model is wrong, which way should each weight move? The answer is the slope: how fast the output changes when you nudge the input. Take a small step against the slope, repeat, and you have gradient descent, the way LLMs are trained.

Chapters
0:00 What a slope measures
0:26 The derivative: the slope at one point
0:41 Step against the slope: gradient descent
1:06 The gradient: one slope per weight
1:17 Slopes multiply: the chain rule and backprop
1:40 Gradient descent in code

episodes.title: Neural Networks in Three Minutes | How LLMs Work: Foundations F12
episodes.description:
Neurons, layers, weights, and learning.

Study guide for this lesson (PDF): https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos/blob/main/foundations/study/f12_study.pdf
All lessons, study guides and source code: https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos

This video has one big idea: a neural network is just a function, built from one very simple part repeated many times. A neuron weighs its inputs, adds a bias and bends the result; neurons side by side make a layer, and stacked layers make a network. Its numbers, the parameters, are not written by anyone: they are learned from data.

Chapters
0:00 A neuron: weigh, add, bend
0:42 A layer is one matrix multiplication
0:54 Stacking layers · Parameters: the numbers that learn

episodes.title: PyTorch and Autograd | How LLMs Work: Foundations F13
episodes.description:
How one line computes every gradient.

Study guide for this lesson (PDF): https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos/blob/main/foundations/study/f13_study.pdf
All lessons, study guides and source code: https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos

This video opens up the one line that does all the calculus in training: loss.backward(). PyTorch records every operation on a tensor as a graph, then walks that graph in reverse with the chain rule. One call fills in the gradient of every weight, and an optimizer uses those gradients to update the weights.

Chapters

0:31 The forward pass builds a graph
0:45 backward(): the chain rule in reverse
1:04 One backward call, every gradient

episodes.title: Train vs Validation Data | How LLMs Work: Foundations F14
episodes.description:
How we know a model really learned.

Study guide for this lesson (PDF): https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos/blob/main/foundations/study/f14_study.pdf
All lessons, study guides and source code: https://github.com/luilan/educational-videos

This video answers one question: how do we know a model has really learned, and not just memorized? Before training we split the data, never train on one slice, the validation set, and measure the loss there too. Comparing the two losses tells us whether the model is learning or overfitting.

Chapters
0:00 A low training loss can fool us
0:26 Split the data before training
0:50 Two losses, and the gap between them
1:13 Overfitting
1:25 The test set: one final, honest score · The split in code
